one_liner: Go XXH64 with scalar amd64/arm64 assembly; about 1.2-1.4x its own pure-Go build from 16 B up, slower at 4 B.
what_it_does: Implements the 64-bit xxHash (XXH64) for Go: Sum64([]byte), Sum64String(string) without a copy, and a streaming Digest that implements hash.Hash64, with NewWithSeed/ResetWithSeed (since v2.3.0) and MarshalBinary/UnmarshalBinary for checkpointing. Output is bit-identical to reference XXH64 (hard-coded test vectors in xxhash_test.go). The assembly is selected automatically on amd64 and arm64 with the gc compiler; the purego build tag (the baseline here) swaps in the Go code behind the same API.
how_it_is_fast: No SIMD: XXH64's four independent 64-bit lanes are already instruction-level parallel, and the assembly simply keeps the four accumulators, the input pointer and the prime constants in registers across the 32-byte block loop with no bounds checks (amd64: IMULQ/ROLQ; arm64: LDP paired loads, fused MADD multiply-add, ROR). The gain over Go compiler output comes from register allocation and instruction selection, so it shrinks as the compiler improves; a non-inlinable assembly call costs more than it saves on 4-byte inputs.
when_to_use: Go services hashing byte slices or strings of 16 B and up on amd64 or arm64: cache keys, sharding and consistent hashing, Bloom filters, deduplication, content checksums (it is the hash behind Prometheus, InfluxDB, VictoriaMetrics, Badger, Ristretto and FreeCache per the README).
You need XXH64 values that match other languages' xxHash (C Cyan4973/xxhash, zstd frame checksums), not a process-local hash.
Bulk throughput on KB-to-MB buffers, where the README shows 16.7-17.3 GB/s against 11.7-12.0 GB/s for the pure-Go build on a Xeon Platinum 8252C.
Streaming input or resumable hashing: Digest accepts incremental Writes and serialises its state with MarshalBinary.
when_not_to_use: Tiny keys of about 4 B: the assembly is slower (README 1.2 vs 1.3 GB/s; a 2024 third-party run in issue #44 measured 2.95 vs 2.70 ns per Sum64 call).
You want XXH3, XXH128 or XXH32: only XXH64 exists here (XXH3 requests #52, #60 and #73 and the XXH32 request #83 are closed without adding them).
Adversarial keys (hash flooding) or security uses: XXH64 is non-cryptographic and Sum64 always uses seed 0; use a seeded hash (hash/maphash, or a NewWithSeed Digest) or a cryptographic hash.

Process-local hash tables where any good hash will do: Go's hash/maphash is the natural stdlib alternative, and the README's claim of being much faster than anything in the standard library comes with no numbers.
Other architectures (386, arm, riscv64, wasm, etc.) or -tags purego builds: you get the pure-Go code, which is the baseline itself.

integration.form: module (Go module github.com/cespare/xxhash/v2; small enough to vendor as source)
integration.min_toolchain: go.mod says go 1.11 (README: Go 1.9.7+/1.10.3+ with minimal module compatibility, or Go 1.11+); CI tests Go 1.21.x and 1.22.x
integration.platforms: amd64 and arm64 assembly using baseline instructions only (no CPU feature detection or AVX); pure Go elsewhere, with CI on Linux, macOS and Windows plus 386/arm/arm64 under QEMU
integration.thread_safety: not documented; Sum64 and Sum64String are pure functions of their input, while a Digest holds mutable state and needs one instance per goroutine or external locking

gotchas: The asm advantage has narrowed with newer Go releases and differs by CPU: maintainer issue #44 (open, v3 milestone) proposes deleting the amd64 assembly if it stops winning. Third-party numbers there: Ryzen 7 6800HS with Go 1.22.3 (single runs, not benchstat), pure Go vs asm, 10 MB 15.78 vs 17.65 GB/s (1.12x), 4 KB 15.41 vs 17.42 (1.13x), 100 B 7.18 vs 9.14 (1.27x), 16 B 2.76 vs 4.42 (1.60x), 4 B 1.48 vs 1.36 (asm slower); with Go 1.19 (CPU unstated) +46% at 4 KB and +38% at 10 MB. The README's 1.4x is from Go 1.19.2 on one Xeon (derived from page data).

Benchmark shape: each sub-benchmark hashes one fixed-size, fixed-content buffer in a tight loop (bench_test.go), so branch prediction, cache residency and the tail loops are ideal; mixed-length key streams are not measured. Discarding the result with `_ =` is harmless here because the assembly call cannot be eliminated and the pure-Go Sum64 is too large to inline.

A zero-valued Digest is not ready for writes: call New or Reset first (open issue #65; PRs #89 and #92 to auto-initialise are unmerged). Sum64 has no seed argument; seeds exist only on Digest, and the seed API is under reconsideration for v3 (#78).

Slices built with unsafe whose capacity is smaller than their length panic in the pure-Go path's three-index slicing (issue #76: 'slice bounds out of range [::40] with capacity 0', traced to a data race and unsafe conversion in the caller), while the assembly path does not check.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Among the catalogued Go-assembly siblings, lukechampine/blake3, zeebo/blake3 and minio/md5-simd are cryptographic hashes with SIMD and larger gains over their pure-Go fallbacks; pick cespare/xxhash when you need a fast non-cryptographic 64-bit hash that matches the XXH64 spec (C reference: Cyan4973/xxhash), and a BLAKE3 sibling when collision resistance against an attacker matters.
verified_claims_summary: Sum64 throughput from the README, measured with go test -benchtime 500ms -count 15 summarised by benchstat, Go 1.19.2, Ubuntu 20.04, Intel Xeon Platinum 8252C, assembly vs the same package with -tags purego: 1.2 vs 1.3 GB/s at 4 B, 3.5 vs 2.9 at 16 B, 8.1 vs 6.9 at 100 B, 16.7 vs 11.7 at 4 KB and 17.3 vs 12.0 GB/s at 10 MB. A 2024 third-party run with Go 1.22.3 on a Ryzen 7 6800HS (issue #44) shows a smaller 1.12-1.13x at 4 KB and 10 MB.
status_note: Quiet since the 2024-07-03 commit (last tag v2.3.0, 2024-04-04) with seven open PRs, including an unmerged AVX-512 path (#79) that the maintainer will not take at the cost of small-input or non-AVX-512 speed; MIT-licensed, dependency-free, small and widely used, so it is safe to depend on or vendor as is.
